title: Coming back well
hookLine: a forest monk who returns to the community should come back with respect

lines: GULISSĀNI COMES IN FROM THE FOREST.
cards: You've been away: six months working remotely, a semester abroad, a long stretch caring for a parent in another city. Now you're walking back into the office, the class, the family dinner. Everyone has moved on a bit.
There are new jokes you don't get. And there's a quiet temptation to come back as the one who's been somewhere. A monk named Gulissāni lived alone in the forest.
One day he comes into the monastery on some business, and Sāriputta takes the chance to give a talk on how to come back.

teach.b: Sāriputta doesn't scold Gulissāni. He speaks to the room. A forest monk who comes back to the community, he says, should be respectful and deferential toward his companions.
If he isn't, people will say: what good is all his solitude, if he can't treat his fellow monks with respect? Then come the details, and they're wonderfully ordinary.

teach.h: WHERE YOU SIT, WHEN YOU ARRIVE.
teach.b: Be skilled about where you sit: don't push in on the elders, and don't push the younger monks off their seats. Don't go into the village too early, or come back too late.
Don't drop in on families before or after the meal. Don't be restless or fidgety. Don't chatter.
Be easy to correct. Guard your senses, eat in moderation, stay awake and mindful. Know the teaching, too: people will ask the forest monk about it.
Every item ends the same way: if he doesn't, some will say, what's the use of his forest life?
Then Moggallāna asks: is this only for forest monks? No, says Sāriputta. It's even more so for those who live near a village.

Nothing in the sutta speaks against the forest. The point is that solitude is tested in company. Whatever you gained alone shows up in where you sit, when you arrive, and how well you take correction.
Coming back well isn't a performance of humility. It's where the time away shows.

how: In Theravada forest lineages, monks may spend stretches in solitude and then return to the monastery for communal occasions, where seating follows seniority and courtesy to fellow monastics is expected.

o: a vow of silence kept in the forest
the robe a forest monk wears in the village

s: Sāriputta scolds Gulissāni by name in front of everyone
he speaks to the gathering about how any forest monk should return.
the advice includes where to sit
don't push in on elders, and don't push the younger monks off their seats.
the sutta says solitude is a waste of time
nothing in it speaks against the forest; it says solitude is tested in how you treat others.

games.q: a forest monk comes back to the monastery. the seats are full. what does Sāriputta's talk advise?
o: sit with the elders; he's earned it
don't push in on elders or push the younger ones off
games.why: be skilled about seating: neither crowding the elders nor displacing the juniors. small courtesy shows what solitude taught.

practice: Picture a group you'll walk back into soon, a team, a class, a family table, and see yourself arriving: where you sit, who you listen to before telling your own news, who's newer that you could make room for.
Keep the picture small and practical, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Garava. Sāriputta's advice to a forest monk returning to the community: respect, good timing, easy to correct. Solitude tested in company.

orig.note: Pali gārava: respect, reverence. the first thing Sāriputta asks of a returning forest monk.

carryVoice: Your line: come back well. Respect first, then the news. That's day four hundred sixty-one.
